questions: What are the p99 spikes tied to?
Can we enable persistent KV cache across batches?
How would dedicated slots reduce unit cost?
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-08 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Meyers (Redwood AE), Priya Anand (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Verdexa Head of ML), Elena Rodriguez (Verdexa Platform), Tom Liu (Verdexa CTO), Nadia Khan (Verdexa SRE)

[00:00] Jordan Meyers: hey everyone thanks for joining uh we've got the sprint readout today, couple of slides and then the deep bench numbers. we only have 45, 50 minutes so we'll try to be sharp.
[00:12] Samir Patel: yeah thanks jordan, appreciate it. want to get straight into the numbers, we did the baseline run last night and noticed a weird p99 hump at around 75% CPU util.
[00:22] Priya Anand: okay so quick context — we ran three profiles: short prompt baseline (≈20 tokens), medium (≈120 tokens), and long (≈512 tokens). benchmarking environment notes: dev lab GPUs, mixed load generator, about 250 rps peak for the simulated user shape.
[00:36] Elena Rodriguez: to call out, our production profile is mostly short + medium, so the short prompt numbers matter most.
[00:44] Luis Ortega: quick callout — warm cache vs cold: when KV cache warm the per-token cost drops and latency improves substantially, but cold starts add 50-120ms depending on sequence length.
[00:55] Tom Liu: are you seeing the same cold-start delta on the incumbent?
[01:00] Priya Anand: slightly different. the incumbent tends to have a steadier p50 but their p99 is worse on short prompts under burst loads, that's what we're trying to show. in our run median for short prompts was 28ms p50 vs incumbent 36ms, p95 74ms vs 85ms, but p99 spiked to 310ms in one 10-minute window when batching throttled.
[01:18] Samir Patel: 310ms is, okay that's noticeable for us. users notice that.
[01:22] Priya Anand: agreed, and digging in we saw a queueing behavior in the batcher at high concurrent requests — when autoscaler didn't add a slot quickly enough, we saw longer batching windows that caused a tail spike. we pushed a config that reduced the max batch wait to 8ms and that dropped p99 to about 150-170ms in subsequent runs.
[01:36] Jordan Meyers: (interrupting) to add — the cost per token during the same peak was about 12% lower on Redwood because of the continuous batching and quantization profile we used; but that only holds if you accept slightly higher p95 under certain burst patterns.
[01:48] Nadia Khan: curious about quantization. are you using int8 across the board? does that change accuracy for our health prompts?
[01:54] Priya Anand: good question — we used an 8-bit quant profile for the medium model variant in the pilot. quality diffs measured on your eval set: ROUGE-ish style metrics showed <0.8% delta for generation acceptance; some edge cases hit lexical mismatches but not meaningfully different per the manual review. we can run a focused quality pass on your 1k prompt set.
[02:14] Samir Patel: please do that, we can't accept a regression for clinical triage phrases.
[02:18] Priya Anand: totally — that's on the next steps.
[02:20] [02:30] Luis Ortega: back on throughput — when we force fully-warmed KV caches and allow continuous batching we achieved 1.8x tokens/sec throughput vs the incumbent's config in the same lab, but that requires keeping a hot cache which uses memory and has an effect on slot sizing.
[02:45] Elena Rodriguez: what's the memory delta? we have limited headroom per node.
[02:49] Priya Anand: roughly +15% RAM per pod for aggressive prefetching + cache retention. you can trade off retention time vs hit rate; we tuned to a 15min retention for the test which hit ~78% cache-hit for your trace.
[03:05] Tom Liu: are there any network implications for your warm cache approach? we run in a VPC with strict egress policies.
[03:11] Jordan Meyers: network is normal — cache lives local to the serving process; only model shards fetch from object store during load. we do need an allowlist for control-plane telemetry in private deployments, but for dedicated/private we can support an air-gapped-ish config.
[03:25] Samir Patel: security — quick check, we saw SOC2 in the docs but is there any SOC2 type II report?
[03:30] Jordan Meyers: yes we have SOC2 Type II and can share a redacted report through the secure doc portal, also we support SAML/SSO and KMS-based key management for Private deployments.
[03:41] Nadia Khan: audit logs retention?
[03:43] Jordan Meyers: adjustable, default 90 days for the hosted tier, enterprise add-on for longer retention.
[03:48] [04:00] Priya Anand: heading back to p99 spikes — in the 48-hour runner we propose to collect flamegraphs and the runtime traces; we saw the batching window expand in two cases: (1) sustained burst causing queueing, (2) a model reload event that briefly paused the worker. we have a mitigation: staggered reloads and a model readiness check that keeps old workers serving until new warm.
[04:25] Samir Patel: model reloads — are those happening frequently in your infra?
[04:29] Priya Anand: not during steady state, but during our stress tests with autoscaling churn we triggered a reload because of ephemeral slot reboots; prod deploys won't churn like that but it's real in lab.
[04:36] Elena Rodriguez: what about fallback routing? i've seen notes about routing to a smaller model with lower latency when heavy — how seamless is that?
[04:41] Luis Ortega: you can do policy-based routing: route by latency SLO or cost. we showed the canary before — fallback is a model variant with smaller context or quantized one; responses degrade slightly in detail but latency improves. there's a delta for hallucination risk with smaller models so you need guardrails.
[04:58] Tom Liu: and how do you measure quality regressions during fallback?
[05:01] Priya Anand: we recommend a two-track monitoring: synthetic prompt set acceptance rates + sampling of real traffic for human-in-loop QA. we can integrate with your existing eval pipeline.
[05:14] [05:30] Jordan Meyers: quick note on economics — dedicated slots reduce per-token cost by ~25% in our estimates for steady 24/7 workloads, because you amortize GPUs. Pilot pricing we proposed includes a reserved cap and burst pool.
[05:44] Samir Patel: that aligns with what the finance team wants to see. Tom, any questions on the cost side?
[05:49] Tom Liu: just want the math and commitment windows, send that sheet.
[05:52] Jordan Meyers: will do, you'll get the sheet today.
[05:55] [06:00] Priya Anand: returning to the data — i have a snippet from the 3pm run last night: at 250 rps simulated short prompt load, Redwood p50=28ms p95=72ms p99 median-day=145ms; incumbent p50=36ms p95=85ms p99=220-420ms depending on the interval. the spread for incumbent was higher at 80-95% traffic intervals. we also instrumented token counts and saw Redwood used fewer tokens due to stop-token heuristics configured.
[06:28] Elena Rodriguez: can you share those raw CSVs?
[06:30] Priya Anand: yes raw logs will be in the share link — we'll drop them in the folder after this call.
[06:35] Samir Patel: in your 1.8x throughput claim, is that with the same GPU types?
[06:39] Luis Ortega: yes same instance types, same model weights; difference is kernel selection + compilation path and continuous batching. also the incumbent used a single-precision path while we used a mixed-int8 kernel on some layers.
[06:50] Samir Patel: does mixed int8 change inference determinism? we need reproducible outputs for audit.
[06:55] Priya Anand: determinism is slightly affected in rare floating point edge cases; we can force FP32 for audited paths, though cost goes up. decision is usually: FP32 for critical audit endpoints, int8 for general queries.
[07:09] [07:30] Jordan Meyers: quick usability note — the console traces show token-level latency breakdown and cost per token. you can filter by route and see the proportion of time spent in KV cache vs attention kernel vs batching.
[07:44] Nadia Khan: will the console be accessible from our VPC?
[07:48] Jordan Meyers: yes via the private control plane in Private deployments; for Dedicated we can create an SSO integration and network peering.
[07:56] [08:00] Samir Patel: walk me through the 48-hour plan you propose.
[08:03] Priya Anand: plan: run parallel clients hitting Redwood and IncumbentAI with identical traces, rotate traffic shapes every 6 hours to exercise short/medium/long prompts, collect p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cache-hit ratios, model-reload events, and autoscaler churn. include instrumentation: trace ids so you can correlate events back to your logs. deliverables: raw logs, summary CSVs, flamegraphs, and a short recommendations doc.
[08:28] Elena Rodriguez: do you need any special access or can we mirror the traffic from our staging cluster?
[08:33] Priya Anand: preferred: you mirror staging traffic via replay to the lab env; otherwise we can drive synthetic traffic from our harness. replay gives more realistic cache-hit profiles.
[08:42] Samir Patel: we'll try replay. we'll need guidance on tokenization differences — i remember a tokenization delta in earlier pilot.
[08:48] Luis Ortega: we'll supply a tokenizer shim and a small script to normalize tokens between systems.
[08:52] [09:00] Tom Liu: on the subject of deployment modes — if we go Dedicated, how quickly can you provision slots? we may want a short lead for the production pilot.
[09:05] Jordan Meyers: provisioning for Dedicated typically 7-10 days once contract signed, less with fast-lane enterprise onboarding. for Private (VPC) it's a bit longer due to networking work, usually 2-4 weeks depending on IP allowlist and KMS setup.
[09:21] Samir Patel: that's fine, timeline wise we'd like to ramp pilot in June.
[09:25] Jordan Meyers: good, that works.
[09:28] [09:30] Priya Anand: minor triage point — we noticed a small number of encoding mismatches from Verdexa's JSON prompts where escaped Unicode triggered a fallback path in our tokenizer, adding ~30ms. we logged examples in the share and suggest normalizing JSON or passing a pre-tokenized field.
[09:48] Elena Rodriguez: we can clean that in the ingest pipeline quickly. thanks for flagging.
[09:52] [10:00] Luis Ortega: competitor note: CloudVendorX uses a different batching strategy that favors latency for single-request cases but doesn't scale tokens/sec as well; we can produce a head-to-head if you want.
[10:13] Samir Patel: we mostly care about incumbent but include a quick CloudVendorX throw-in if easy.
[10:17] Jordan Meyers: sure we'll include CloudVendorX as a light comparator.
[10:20] [10:30] Action recap segment:
[10:33] Jordan Meyers: recap of owners: priya runs 48h, jordan sends pricing, samir shares prompt set, elena confirms VPC details. we'll follow up with a calendar invite for May 19th to review the 48h results.
[10:47] Samir Patel: sounds good. one more question — in the event of a regression in the 48h run, do you have automatic rollback/in-flight fallbacks?
[10:56] Priya Anand: yes we can configure automatic fallback policies based on SLO thresholds that route to the incumbent model variant or a smaller Redwood variant; plus we have canary rollouts and immediate roll-back triggers.
[11:07] Tom Liu: okay that's reassuring.
[11:09] Jordan Meyers: anything else from Verdexa?
[11:12] Nadia Khan: just please include the trace correlation IDs in the logs so our SREs can map events.
[11:16] Priya Anand: will include trace IDs and span IDs in the CSVs.
[11:19] Samir Patel: alright thanks everyone.
[11:22] Jordan Meyers: thanks all — we'll send the share link and pricing by EOD and set up the 48h run. talk soon.

End of meeting.
